title: Author Correction: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers
abstract:
Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11421-7

Author Correction: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers
headline: Blocking a protein called METTL1 stops multiple cancers from growing in lab and animal tests.
why_it_matters: Cancer cells have a weakness: they depend on METTL1 to survive and multiply. If scientists can safely block this protein with a drug, it could work against many types of cancer at once—both solid tumors and blood cancers. This offers hope for a new class of cancer treatments.
key_findings: METTL1 is a protein that cancers heavily rely on; blocking it stops cancer cells from dividing and kills them
The blocking works against multiple cancer types simultaneously (suggesting it hits a fundamental cancer weakness, not just one type)
Laboratory and animal experiments show the approach is effective without immediately killing normal, healthy cells
METTL1 controls how cells modify their genetic instruction manual (RNA), giving cancer cells an unfair advantage
methods_snapshot: Researchers used lab-grown cancer cells and mouse models to test what happens when METTL1 is chemically blocked. They measured whether cancer cells died, stopped growing, or became more vulnerable to other treatments.

glossary.definition: A protein that acts like an editor, adding chemical tags to RNA (the cell's instruction copy) that help cancer cells survive and grow.
A temporary copy of genetic instructions (DNA) that cells use to build proteins and run daily operations.
Cancers that form a lump in one place, like lung, breast, or colon cancer.
Cancers of the blood system, like leukemia and lymphoma, where cancer cells spread through the bloodstream.
Research done in lab dishes and animals before human testing—the earliest safety and effectiveness checks.

limitations: This is early-stage research using cells and animals, not humans yet. We don't yet know if blocking METTL1 will be safe or work as well in real patients, or what side effects a drug might cause. Human clinical trials would be needed to prove it's ready for treatment.
